newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - HSBC says Mexican bank deal complementary.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - HSBC says Mexican bank deal complementary.

text.p: International banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc said on Wednesday that buying a stake in Mexico's Grupo Financiero Serfin would complement its existing presence in the Asia-Pacific region and the United States.

"It is a natural complement to our franchise on the Asian side of the Pacific Rim and to our U.S. presence," George Cardona, General Manager International at Midland Bank, part of the HSBC group, told Reuters.
HSBC agreed in principle on Tuesday to buy a 19.9 percent stake for around $300 million in Mexico's third-largest banking group, which lost more than $800 million in 1996.

Cardona said HSBC was confident of the prospects for both Serfin -- which had inherited a good franchise -- and the Mexican economy, which had been greatly boosted by the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
"NAFTA has really made a difference and is making a difference to the Mexican economy," Cardona said, adding that he believed Mexico had been well run after the 1995 financial crisis.
The deal is not expected to go through until later in the year but Cardona said full terms would be disclosed "in due course".
It is seen as a crucial step in pulling Serfin out of a prolonged crisis. It has been plagued by bad loans and steep losses since Mexico's economy crashed in December 1994.
HSBC has a long-standing presence in Latin America. It already has stakes in banks in Chile, Argentina, Panama and most recently Peru.
But in buying the Serfin stake, HSBC is not marking an intention to take a larger holding. "We have no plans at this stage," Cardona said.
Serfin reported a 1996 loss of some $880 million, mainly the result of creating more than $1 billion in reserves to cover unpaid loans that have almost drained the bank dry in the last two years.
It also announced that the Mexican government would become a shareholder in the bank, taking a stake for some $250 million.
In exchange, Serfin sold some $1.3 billion in problem mortgage loans to the government. This was described as one of its final efforts to clear up the bank's default-plagued loan portfolio.
The sale to HSBC must be approved by both banks' shareholders and board members and Serfin must also raise more capital, which it plans to do by selling its insurance unit.
To complete the sale, HSBC will buy some $290 million convertible subordinated debentures that Serfin issued to J.P. Morgan in July 1996.
HSBC is expected to have representatives on the Serfin board, but will leave the present management to run the bank, providing technical assistance when and where it is required.

HSBC will not only bring retail banking expertise to the Mexican bank, it will also inject its experience of trade finance and particularly its knowledge of trans-Pacific business. The know-how of HSBC Investment Banking is also likely to be drawn upon once the relationship is sealed.

As well as the fact that Serfin was putting its troubled past behind it, personalities were also crucial to HSBC's decision to take a stake in it. Cardona said Serfin's chief executive Adolfo Lagos had been a key factor in the choice.
"One of the reasons why we wanted to invest in the bank was his very high reputation in the Mexican market and our own confidence in him," he said.
Serfin has some 600 branches and assets of $20 billion in Mexico. HSBC has over 3,800 offices in 78 countries, with assets at the end of last year of $402 billion.
